title: My health isn’t a loyalty program

A clear chart can still leave a question unanswered This belongs in the brief Let me correct my very personal app The relationship should leave me with something useful Product Design UX Design Product Management Digital Health Health Technology My health isn’t a loyalty program What product designers and managers should ask before celebrating the next visit. Iris Atalay 5 min read · Just now -- Listen Share I read Allen Adamson’s Forbes article about Apple and Google competing to become our everyday health companions. The headline says the winner “owns you for life.” For life? Okay. I would like to read the relationship agreement first. Adamson argues that meaningful outcomes build lasting relationships. He also warns about privacy, nagging, and turning health into a sales funnel. I agree. My question is what those promises require from the people designing the app. I’ve spent 17 years in product design, working in health and wellness since 2021: first at Playbook, then Nutrisense, and now Dexcom after it acquired Nutrisense. From the design side, I want that relationship to give people useful support and real choices. We need to decide what the app should help them do before celebrating how often they use it. Yes, I would like an app that remembers me Continuity can be valuable. Having to reconnect information or explain the same history to another service takes effort. Someone managing an ongoing condition may need regular support for years. Apple’s September announcement describes a redesigned Health app planned for later in 2026. Google’s October update describes improved Coach memory and deeper Apple Health integration. More context, less starting from zero. I understand the appeal. I would quite like useful help without introducing myself to my own app every morning. Retention matters to keeping that service running. It still needs interpreting. They came back. Why? Imagine two people returning to a health app. One comes back because yesterday’s explanation helped. The other still doesn’t understand yesterday’s result and hopes another look will help. Our dashboard can count both visits. As designers, we need to find out which experience we created. Press enter or click to view image in full size The same return visit can have different reasons. Frequent use can be helpful, and fewer visits wouldn’t automatically mean a better experience. We need to understand what the person came back for. A clear chart can still leave a question unanswered Imagine someone looking at a change on a glucose chart. They can read the number and see when it happened. They still want to know what it means for them. That question needs careful handling. What context does the app actually have? What is missing? Can it offer a useful explanation within its scope, or does the question need a qualified professional? Press enter or click to view image in full size A readable chart still needs context, clear limits, and an appropriate next step. A Google-led study published in Nature in October makes a useful distinction. The team evaluated a prototype health agent through benchmark tasks and conversations assessed by participants and experts. The authors describe evidence of conversational quality and short-term task performance, rather than sustained behaviour change or long-term health improvement. A helpful explanation, someone understanding it, and a health improvement are different things to establish. Our product conversations should be clear about which one we have evidence for. This belongs in the brief Before designing an insight, I want the team to name its intended benefit. Help someone interpret a pattern? Find suitable support? Know whether any action is needed? Then we can test the understanding that particular decision requires. I don’t expect everyone to become an expert in their own charts. Sometimes the useful result is getting appropriate help with less effort. Suppose we add an explanation below a glucose chart and repeat views increase. Before adding another reminder, I’d ask people what they returned to find and observe whether they could find it. If they’re still trying to resolve the same question, I’d revise the explanation or the route to suitable support first. Another reminder won’t make the first explanation clearer. If people understand the essential limits and return for useful new context, that changes the decision. Regular use may be doing exactly what they need. If we changed the flow, I’d compare it with the original: can people reach the intended answer or support with less effort, without introducing new misunderstandings? For human support, that includes knowing who they’ll speak to, what that person can help with, and what they’re agreeing to. Whether the support was useful needs follow-up. As a manager, I want the intended benefit and those checks in the brief, with relevant clinical, engineering, and privacy colleagues involved early. The research needs to be able to change the next design decision. Let me correct my very personal app Memory sounds wonderful until the coach remembers something incorrectly, or keeps using a preference I changed three months ago. Where do I fix that? I’m allowed to change my mind. We did say personal, right? Correcting a preference and spotting incorrect health advice are different problems. I can tell an app what I prefer. I may not know enough to judge its explanation of my health. A September JMIR study looked at how people judged AI-generated health information. Across two experiments, greater self-reported dependency on AI was associated with weaker discrimination between correct and incorrect health information when rating trust.
